title: Soft commit lifecycle and eviction mitigation — PRD (rough)
body:
Purpose and intent

This doc is a rough PRD for a "soft commit" lifecycle for Dedicated capacity customers. The idea: provide a user-visible reservation model that reduces hard eviction spikes and improves predictability for mid-sized tenants who need guaranteed baseline throughput but can tolerate transient scaledown if they opt into negotiated degradation. The goal is to reduce emergency evictions and noisy-neighbor incidents while preserving the economic and operational benefits of reserved capacity.

Why this problem matters
- We frequently see churn in dedicated pools when multiple tenants hit unexpected simultaneous peaks. Hard preemption leads to customer-facing latency spikes and subsequent support escalations.
- Customers want stronger SLA-like assurances than best-effort bursts, but they also want cheaper commitments than full dedicated slices for peak usage.
- Existing solutions (static soft-eviction windows, blunt throttles) either wipe performance too aggressively or fail to prevent queue crush.

Proposed product concept (high level)
- Soft commit: a reservation contract that exposes three phases for each reservation period: committed baseline, flexible buffer, and opportunistic pool. Each phase has different guarantees, pricing, and preemption behavior.
- Lifecycle controller: an internal controller that transitions reservations across states based on observed utilization, predictive forecasts, and cross-tenant demand signals.
- Eviction mitigation suite: staged degradation techniques (graceful shedding, request pacing, capped concurrency) and fallback routing (lower-cost model variants, region/zone fallback) to avoid sudden evictions.

Customer-facing UX / API
- New reservation type: POST /reservations with payload fields: baseline_units, flexible_buffer_units, preempt_priority (low/medium/high), degradation_policy (pause|throttle|fallback_model), commit_window (monthly|quarterly|annual).
- UI: Console shows a timeline of reservation state (Active -> BufferBorrowed -> BorrowCooldown -> SoftDegraded). Real-time headroom indicator and an "expected eviction risk" badge driven by demand forecasts.
- Billing: baseline charged at reservation rate; flexible_buffer charged at a modest incremental rate but with explicit preemption terms; opportunistic usage billed at on-demand rates. Credits/penalties for overcommit behavior documented in contract.

Internal behavior and autoscaling integration
- Controller inputs: per-tenant token throughput, latency SLO breach rate, model mix, historical peak patterns, upcoming commit windows, and global capacity signals.
- Autoscaling decisions are made with buckets: maintain baseline always; allow buffer consumption if global headroom > threshold X; if demand rises above threshold Y trigger controlled degradation flow rather than immediate eviction.
- Prediction: short-horizon (10–60m) peak detection uses EWMA + anomaly flags; longer-horizon (6–48h) uses trend extrapolation and calendar signals (scheduled jobs).

Eviction mitigation techniques (ordered escalation)
1) Suggest alternate model variant: route excess requests to a quantized/4-bit variant when acceptable.
2) Prefix caching and KV reuse: prioritize reuse of cached contexts to reduce token compute.
3) Pacing and queuing: introduce per-tenant pacing with SLA-weighted priorities.
4) Soft SLAs: reduce per-request token budget or max concurrency for flexible buffer consumers.
5) Graceful preemption: if all else fails, place requests into a short (30s–2m) wait window with user-visible 429-retry-after and telemetry tags.
6) Hard preempt (last resort): evict opportunistic and then buffer units to preserve baseline.

Operational controls and SRE runbook (ops-oriented)
- Monitoring: add dedicated dashboards for soft-commit lanes — headroom, buffer consumption rate, risk score, soft-degrade count, graceful-fallbacks applied.
- Alerts: page on: (a) soft-degrade count rising > 10% tenants in 10m, (b) prediction confidence dropping while risk score > 0.7, (c) failed graceful-fallbacks > 5% of requests.
- Runbook steps for high-risk events: 1) identify top consumers, 2) throttle opportunistic lanes, 3) temporarily increase warm pool for critical models (if available), 4) coordinate with account team for customer communication, 5) backfill with reserve capacity if contractual.

Acceptance criteria and metrics
- Functional: reservation API accepts soft_commit params; controller transitions states reliably in staging; console shows risk indicator.
- SLOs: baseline throughput available 99.95% of the time; soft degrade incidents do not produce hard evictions in 95% of simulated simultaneous-peaks tests.
- Economic: average monthly cost/tenant under soft-commit to be >= 10% cheaper than equivalent full-slice reservation for typical mid-sized tenants.
- Operational: mean time to detect and apply graceful fallback < 60s in production traffic tests.

Design considerations / tradeoffs
- Complexity vs transparency: more nuanced preemption policies help reliability but make billing and SLAs harder to explain. We must keep the console messaging explicit ("What you'll pay, and when you can be degraded").
- Predictive risk errors: false positives cause unnecessary throttling; false negatives cause evictions. We'll tune conservatively in first rollout.
- Multi-tenant fairness: controller must weigh customer tier and commit windows; implement a simple scoring function first (priority * commit_size / recent_usage) before more complex market mechanisms.

Data & telemetry needed
- Per-request tags for reservation id, commit phase, fallback_applied boolean, latency pre- and post-fallback, token_count, model_variant.
- Aggregates: buffer consumption per-minute, top-k buffer consumers, predictive risk signals, eviction-reduction delta vs baseline.

Rollout plan (phases)
- Phase 0 (internal): implement controller in staging, basic API, and simulated traffic harness. Target 2 sprints.
- Phase 1 (canary): opt-in for internal Redwood teams and 3 pilot customers. Monitor metrics for 30 days.
- Phase 2 (beta): expose soft-commit to select new customers via console toggle; limit total buffer capacity to 15% of pool for 60 days.
- Phase 3 (general): open to all tenants, enable per-tenant tuning UI, add pricing docs and contract addendum.

Open questions / decisions to make
- Pricing structure for buffer units: fixed uplift vs dynamic market price? Recommend fixed uplift for predictability initially.
- Should we expose per-request retry semantics vs hiding it behind automatic retry? Need legal/contract review for user-visible retry implications.
- How to handle cross-region fallback for private deployments with strict data locality? Likely need a variant that keeps compute local but uses smaller models.

Risks and mitigations
- Customer confusion: mitigate with simple default policies and clear console language; craft onboarding emails for pilot customers.
- Billing disputes: add detailed telemetry export (CSV/Confluence) for each soft-degrade event.
- Model-quality regressions when routed to quantized variants: provide auto-eval hooks to allow customers to specify "do not downgrade for X prompts" lists.

Notes to self / next actions
- Sync with pricing leads (Priya) to finalize buffer uplift numbers.
- Ask infra team (Ethan) to prototype predictive headroom signal telemetry.
- Draft pilot customer briefing and runbook for CS / AMs.

Appendix (short snippets)
- Example API sketch:
  POST /v1/dedicated/reservations
  body: { baseline_units: 10, flexible_buffer_units: 4, preempt_priority: "medium", degradation_policy: "throttle", commit_window: "monthly" }
- Example console copy for risk badge:
  "Eviction risk: Low/Medium/High — based on current pool headroom and scheduled commitments. Click to see mitigation steps we will apply if capacity tightens."

This is intentionally a rough draft. Want feedback on the scoring heuristic and the proposed staged escalation. If we converge, I will turn this into a formal PRD with diagrams, API schema, and a simulated test plan.
